Select a result row to inspect its mask preview. Check boundaries, touching objects and missed objects against the image. Use the object count and quality flags to help find fields that need closer inspection.

Review the field summaries, then keep the chosen checkpoint path for your analysis module. To compare two different model families on the same images, select both rows and choose Compare the two selected. Use the version control to try another version of one family.

lessons.title: Annotator Agreement: compare independent annotation passes
lessons.description: Choose annotation columns, compare agreement and inspect the crops where labels differ.
objectives: Open the example database and select two annotation passes.
Read pairwise agreement and the confusion matrix.
Inspect disagreements and compare three annotation passes.
lessons.prerequisite: Extract the linked Annotator Agreement example and keep its database with the crop images. It contains sixteen images from the Annotate example and three artificial teaching-label columns, DEMO_A, DEMO_B and DEMO_C. For your own analysis, use independently collected annotations of the same images.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Annotate, then choose Annotator Agreement. Use this tool to compare labels collected in separate annotation passes. The results help you find images that need review.

Open the example database. Keep the extracted crop folders beside it so the image previews can load. The DEMO columns contain artificial teaching labels; use your own independent annotation columns when assessing agreement in a study.
Select at least two annotation columns from the list. For this example, start with DEMO A and DEMO B. Check the column names so you compare the intended passes.

Click Compute agreement. The two selected passes share twelve labelled crops. Three more crops have a label in only one pass, and one has neither label. Pairwise agreement uses the crops labelled by both passes.

Read the pairwise results. The passes agree on nine of twelve crops, giving seventy-five percent agreement and a Cohen kappa of zero point five. Read these values alongside the number of shared labels; a small sample gives an uncertain estimate.

Open the confusion matrix. Rows represent DEMO A and columns represent DEMO B. The diagonal contains matching labels: five for class one and four for class two. The off-diagonal cells contain the three disagreements.
Select a disagreement to view its crop and the labels assigned by each pass. Compare the image with your class definitions. To revise a label after review, return to Annotate.

Add DEMO C and click Compute agreement again. The pairwise table now shows all three pairs. Each pair uses its shared labels, while the overall summary uses crops labelled in all three selected passes.

Read the overall Fleiss kappa and the unanimous agreement summary. This example gives a Fleiss kappa of about zero point six six three. Review the disagreement list as well: it can include a crop that has labels in only two of the three passes.

To focus on one pair again, select only A and B and click Compute agreement. The results stay in this comparison view; your annotation columns remain in the source database. Continue in Annotate to collect another independent pass or review the identified disagreements.

lessons.title: Plaque Assay: count plaques and measure their areas
lessons.description: Open the synthetic example, choose saved masks or model segmentation, inspect a preview, and read the per-image and per-plaque results.
objectives: Open Plaque Assay from Toxoplasma and select the image folder.
Choose a model, inspect a preview and set area filters.
Run the analysis and inspect counts, areas and calibration in the output database.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and extract SYNTHETIC_plaque_example.zip. It contains four grayscale TIFF images and their saved label masks. Use a working copy when trying new segmentation. Have a local plaque checkpoint available or download one through Model Zoo. The synthetic example has no physical calibration.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Toxoplasma, then choose Plaque Assay. Start with a folder of plaque images. This walkthrough uses the linked synthetic example so you can practise selecting masks, adjusting the preview and opening the results.
Download and extract the example. Set Source to SYNTHETIC_plaque, the folder containing the TIFF images and the masks subfolder. Keep a working copy if you plan to generate replacement masks.

Leave Masks off to analyse the supplied label masks. Switch Masks on when you want the selected model to segment the images first. For new segmentation, choose a plaque model and review its diameter and detection thresholds on a representative image.

Leave well detection off for this example. For images containing a whole plate, use well detection to separate the wells. If you know the image scale, enter pixels per micrometer; a known physical well diameter can also provide calibration. Record formation time in hours when it is known. Leave unknown calibration values unset.

Set Plaque model to a local checkpoint. If you need one, open Model Zoo and download a plaque model, then enter its local path. The analysis resolves this model setting even when it reuses saved masks.
Open Live preview and Live settings. Check the selected model and image before running the preview. Match the model in the preview to the one you plan to use for the full analysis.

In Model Zoo, select the plaque model, choose a Save to folder and click Download. Wait until the model is available locally, then select that checkpoint for the preview. Keep its saved path for later runs.

Choose an example image and click Run preview. Switch View between outlines and coloured masks to check whether the predicted regions follow plaque boundaries. Inspect several representative images before running a plate.

Raise Min area to hide small predicted regions. Watch which objects disappear, and adjust the threshold to the smallest plaque you intend to measure. Change one setting at a time so its effect is clear.

Lower Min area to bring smaller regions back; zero removes this lower area cutoff. Check the final preview and the batch settings before Run. A preview shows the selected image; Run produces the analysis outputs.

Press Run and follow the console until the analysis finishes. With Masks off, the example reads the supplied labels and writes masks/plaques_analysis.db. The database contains the counts and areas for the images in Source.
Open Help, then Database browser. Select plaques_analysis.db in the masks folder. Leave Edit mode off while inspecting the output, and choose a table from the table list.
Open summary for an overview by image. Match rows using their filenames. The supplied synthetic masks contain four, three, two and one objects. Average size reports their mean area in pixels.

Open stats to compare each image’s plaque count, mean area and area spread. The standard deviation describes the range of plaque sizes within that image. Use independent experimental replicates when comparing biological conditions.

Open details to inspect individual plaque areas. Physical-area columns are empty when calibration is unavailable. Save the database together with the images, masks and settings. Experimental growth estimates additionally require a known scale to estimate time, or a known time to estimate scale; validate the reference curve for your assay.

lessons.title: Recruitment: measure marker enrichment around parasites
lessons.description: Choose a measured project, map the marker channel and conditions, set object filters, then inspect recruitment ratios by host cell and well.
objectives: Select a project containing linked cell, nucleus, pathogen and cytoplasm measurements.
Set the marker channel, plate conditions and object filters.
Run Recruitment and read the host-cell and well CSV results.
lessons.prerequisite: Start with a project from Measure containing measurements/measurements.db and linked cell, nucleus, pathogen and cytoplasm tables. Include merged images to display image overlays. The example uses an ER marker on channel 1; use the channel mapping and condition labels recorded for your own project.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Toxoplasma, then choose Recruitment. Use this analysis to compare marker intensity in parasite-associated regions with the surrounding host-cell cytoplasm. Begin with a project whose objects and intensity channels have already been measured.
Set Source to the project folder containing measurements/measurements.db. Keep the cell, nucleus, pathogen and cytoplasm tables together. Include the merged image folder if you want image overlays.

Set Channel of interest to the marker you want to measure. Channels use zero-based numbering: one means the second image plane. This example uses channel one for the ER marker. Choose the channel that matches your acquisition.

Set Channel dims to the channels needed for the auxiliary recruitment summaries. For a first run, use the same single channel as Channel of interest so the main ratio and additional intensity summaries are easy to compare.

Check the cell, nucleus and pathogen channel mapping against the measured project. The example uses cell one, nucleus zero and pathogen three. Keep the mapping with your settings so overlays and filters refer to the intended signals.

Enter the cell, pathogen and treatment labels, then map each label to its plate rows or columns. Only annotated wells enter the analysis. Match these assignments to your plate layout, including the positive and negative controls.

Use the size ranges to exclude objects outside the areas you intend to analyse. Areas are in pixels, and the bounds are strict. Pathogen area is aggregated within each host cell for this analysis, so choose its range for the cell-level total.

Set Nuclei limit and Pathogen limit to control which host cells are retained. A nuclei limit of one keeps single-nucleus cells. Raise a limit to include cells with more associated objects, then inspect how many cells remain.

Start with broad intensity ranges so you can inspect the initial results. Narrow a range when you have a defined intensity-based selection rule. Target intensity minimum applies an additional cutoff to the marker’s cell intensity.

Check the channel used by each intensity filter before narrowing its bounds. With the example’s mapping, the nucleus intensity filter uses channel three and the pathogen intensity filter uses channel one. Keep the broad example ranges while learning the workflow.

Set Cells per well to the minimum source-cell count required for a well to remain in the analysis. This setting filters wells, while the object filters select cells. Inspect the final retained counts as well as the threshold.

Enable Plot to display available image overlays and use Plot number to limit how many are shown. Keep Plot control enabled if you want the control-intensity figures. Use the plots to check channel choices and filtering before interpreting the ratios.

Press Run. Follow the console as the module joins the measurements, applies conditions and filters, calculates ratios and writes the results. Wait until the analysis finishes before opening the output tables.

Inspect the recruitment plot. The main value divides the host cell’s aggregated pathogen mean intensity by its cytoplasm mean intensity on the selected marker channel. Values above one indicate enrichment relative to that reference. Read the numeric exports for ratios below the plotted range or invalid denominators.

Inspect the well summary and compare the control conditions. Each well averages its retained cell ratios; condition plots summarize those well values. Error bars show between-well standard deviation. The cell table represents host cells with aggregated pathogen measurements.

Open results/cells.csv for retained host-cell measurements and results/wells.csv for well summaries. Keep both files with the saved settings. Check cell counts, condition labels and finite ratios before comparing experiments, and use independent wells as the experimental replicates.

lessons.title: Invasion Assay: score outside and total staining
lessons.description: Map two staining channels, choose the staining baseline, run the analysis and inspect invasion calls and threshold sensitivity.
objectives: Choose the measurement database and map outside and total staining.
Set baseline wells and threshold controls, then run the analysis.
Inspect distributions, well denominators and saved result tables.
lessons.prerequisite: Extract the linked synthetic Invasion Assay example and use its settings reference. The database contains 1,800 synthetic parasite measurements; condition names and results are illustrative. For your own assay, use a validated two-colour staining design with outside staining before permeabilisation and total staining afterwards, and review representative images.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Toxoplasma, then choose Invasion Assay. Start with a measurement database containing parasite intensities for the outside and total stains. Use the linked synthetic sample to practise channel mapping, threshold selection and result inspection.

Extract the sample and set Source to its invasion folder, which contains measurements/measurements.db. Enter the accompanying settings reference and replace its Source placeholder. The sample contains baseline wells and two assay conditions.

Set Outside channel to one and Total channel to zero. Outside represents the stain applied before permeabilisation; total represents the stain applied afterwards. Outside-positive parasites are classified as attached, and those at or below the outside threshold as invaded. Check your acquisition channel order when using your own measurements.

Select mean under Intensity statistic to match the columns in the example database. For your own assay, choose an available statistic suited to the stain and inspect representative objects. Keep Minimum total intensity at one hundred for this sample.

Set Stain baseline wells to column one, using c1. These negative-stain measurements establish the cutoff and are excluded from the assay denominators. Under Pathogen plate metadata, map vehicle to column two and inhibitor to column three.

Set Control quantile to zero point nine nine and leave the fixed Outside threshold unset. The baseline measurements then determine the cutoff, about twenty-two point eight in this example. Check the applied threshold in the output before interpreting the classifications.

Set Threshold sensitivity to zero point two five. This also evaluates cutoffs twenty-five percent below and above the selected threshold. Compare the resulting invasion-efficiency range to see how strongly your result depends on threshold choice.

Set Extracellular class to classify for the sample. For objects without a host link, classify uses the stain, attached assigns them to attached, and exclude removes them from the scored population. Choose this setting with the quality of your host-cell assignments in mind.

Keep Save enabled and click Run. Open the threshold figure after processing finishes. It shows distributions by well and the applied cutoff. For an experiment, compare these distributions with representative stained images and investigate weak outside staining.

If a legend extends beyond the figure, open Figure settings. In the axes tab, set Legend position to best, then confirm. Check that the labels remain visible in both the on-screen and exported figures.

Open the per-well figure. Each bar shows attached and invaded fractions, with the number of scored parasites above it. Baseline wells are excluded. Read the counts alongside the fractions when comparing wells.

Open the condition summary. Compare the pooled invasion fraction with the mean across wells, since they use different weighting. Check the per-well results for variation before making comparisons between conditions.

Open results/analyze_invasion inside Source. Review parasite_calls.csv, field_thresholds.csv, well_invasion.csv and condition_summary.csv, together with the saved figures and settings. Use independent experimental replicates when assessing differences in your own assay.

lessons.title: Replication Assay: count parasites per vacuole
lessons.description: Load parasite measurements, choose the vacuole identity, run the analysis and inspect count distributions and exports.
objectives: Choose a measurement database and its vacuole identifier.
Set host-assignment and size filters, then run the analysis.
Read per-well distributions and locate the saved result tables.
lessons.prerequisite: Extract the linked synthetic Replication Assay example. It contains a measurement database and a settings reference, with 1,992 parasite rows in 480 vacuoles across twelve wells. The condition names and measurements are teaching data. For your own assay, use measured parasites with reviewed vacuole assignments and independent experimental replicates.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Toxoplasma, then choose Replication Assay. Start with a measurement database containing parasite rows and their vacuole assignments. The linked synthetic example lets you practise the settings and read the resulting count distributions.

Extract the sample and set Source to its replication folder. The database is inside measurements. Enter the accompanying settings reference, replacing its Source placeholder with your extracted folder. Keep Save enabled to write the results.
Set Vacuole key to vacuole_id. This groups parasites by the vacuole they belong to. The sample contains two vacuoles per host-cell group, so use the vacuole identifier to keep those counts separate.

Enable Require host cell to include only parasites linked to a host cell. Review unassigned objects when using your own data. For this sample, set Minimum parasite area to two hundred and Maximum parasite area to eight hundred.

Set Maximum parasites per vacuole to sixteen. This sets the largest named power-of-two bucket. Larger power-of-two counts go into an overflow bucket, while counts such as three remain in the separate non-power-of-two category.

Enter vehicle and inhibitor as the two Pathogen types, and map them to column one and column two in Pathogen plate metadata. Each group contains six practice wells. For your experiment, enter the condition names and well assignments from your plate design.
Check Source, Vacuole key, filters and Save, then click Run. Follow the console until processing finishes. The Figures area will show distributions by well and by condition.

Open the per-well figure. Each stacked bar shows the fraction of vacuoles in each parasite-count category. Read the colours with the legend. In this sample, each well contains forty vacuoles and five percent fall in the non-power-of-two category.

Open Figure settings to adjust the legend. In the axes tab, choose an inside Legend position if the labels extend beyond the figure. This changes the presentation while retaining the calculated counts.

Open the by-condition figure to compare the pooled count distributions. Inspect the per-well results alongside this summary. When analysing an experiment, use independent biological replicates and a suitable experimental unit for statistical comparisons.
Read any export warnings in the console. Check the saved figures as well as the on-screen view, and choose colours that remain readable against the export background.

Open results/analyze_replication inside Source. Review vacuole_counts.csv for individual vacuoles, well_distribution.csv for each well, and the condition summaries and figures. Keep these outputs with the settings and source database so you can trace the analysis.

lessons.title: Training Runs: compare curves and settings
lessons.description: Load training logs, overlay metrics, compare settings and explore cross-validation folds.
objectives: Find saved runs and select the ones to compare.
Overlay training and validation metrics and inspect settings differences.
Switch between individual folds and their mean and standard deviation.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and extract the linked synthetic Training Runs example. Its curves are practice data. For your own analysis, select a parent folder containing saved train.csv and validation.csv files with each run’s settings. Keep independent evaluation results with your model when assessing performance.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Classify, then Training Runs. Use this tool to compare the progress logs and settings from saved training runs. The linked sample contains synthetic curves for practising the controls.
Training Runs provides a folder selector, run list, Metric menu, Folds menu and Overlay selected button. Begin by choosing the parent folder containing the runs you want to compare.

Extract the linked sample and click Choose folder. Select its training_runs folder, then confirm the choice. For your own projects, select a parent folder containing the run folders and their saved CSV logs.
Scan the folder and inspect the discovered runs. The sample has baseline, tuned and cross_validated examples, plus one incomplete entry. Select the usable runs you want to compare.
Check warnings on incomplete entries. Missing train.csv, validation.csv or settings can prevent curves or settings from appearing. Locate the complete run folder before adding it to a comparison.

Tick baseline and tuned, then choose accuracy under Metric. The menu lists the numeric columns available in the selected logs. Choose loss or another recorded metric when it answers your comparison question.
Click Overlay selected. Training curves are dashed and validation curves are solid. Read each run and split in the legend. Each curve ends at its own final recorded epoch.

Inspect the settings comparison below the plot. It highlights differences such as batch size, epoch count and learning rate. Use it to identify what changed between the runs before interpreting their curves.
The environment row separates execution settings, such as worker count, from training configuration. Read these alongside the configuration differences when comparing runs made on different machines.

Click a validation curve to see its last and best recorded values and epochs. Use the same selection rule when comparing runs. Evaluate a selected checkpoint on independent data to assess its performance.
Choose loss under Metric to update the vertical axis and overlay. Compare the training and validation trajectories, including their direction near the end of training.
Select tuned and cross_validated, choose accuracy, then click Overlay selected. Open Folds and choose whether to display individual folds, their mean and standard deviation, or both.

Choose mean plus or minus standard deviation to summarize the fold curves. Each band shows one sample standard deviation across the available folds at that epoch. Read the band as variation across folds.
Choose both to show the individual fold curves together with their mean. Compare the folds to see whether a summary hides a run with a different trajectory.
Choose per fold to show only the individual curves. The settings comparison updates with your selected runs. Keep each curve’s epoch range in mind when comparing where training ended.
Return to Metric to compare another logged quantity, or change the selected runs to narrow the comparison. Keep the original CSV logs and settings together so the same comparison can be reopened.

For scripted analysis, use find_runs and load_run in spacr.train_compare, then compare_runs and plot_curves. Keep the comparison with your model and independent evaluation results when choosing the next training configuration.

lessons.title: Report: create a document from project results
lessons.description: Choose a completed project, select the output format and figure limit, then generate and read its report.
objectives: Choose a completed project and inspect its available report sections.
Set the format, figure limit and output filename.
Generate the report and inspect its results, settings and provenance.
lessons.prerequisite: Start with a completed spaCR project containing its saved settings, measurements and figures. You can reuse the project from the External Masks tutorial. Report collects files already present in the project.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Report. Use this tool to collect a completed project’s results, figures and settings into a document.
Click Choose run folder and select your project. For this example, use the two-field project from External Masks, keeping its measurements, settings and figures together.
Read the processing status after the scan. Complete means the recorded processing steps finished. Review the available quality-control results separately when assessing the analysis.
Check the section list to see which project artifacts are available. A missing section remains labelled in the report. Add the relevant analysis outputs to the project if you need that section.
Choose HTML, PDF or Both under Format. HTML opens in a browser; PDF provides a document version. This example uses HTML.
Set Embed at most to limit the number of raster figures included in the document. Vector PDFs are listed as source files rather than embedded previews. Use a smaller limit for a compact report.
Click Choose output and enter the destination filename. Check that the selected format and extension agree. Before sharing the report, review any project paths and metadata it includes.
Press Generate report and wait for the written-file confirmation. Open the saved HTML file in a browser to inspect the result.
Use the contents links to jump between sections. Start with the processing summary, then review figures, result tables and saved settings.
Open Key figures to find the project’s figures. Follow the listed file locations for vector PDFs, or inspect embedded raster previews when available.

Review Statistics and result tables for the available object tables and their row counts. This cell-only example has matching cell and cytoplasm regions, so treat them as measurements of the same cells.
Expand Saved settings to inspect the configuration retained with the project. Keep the report together with the project files when sharing an analysis that refers to external figures.

lessons.title: Plate Queue: run several prepared projects
lessons.description: Add the current project or drop prepared folders into a queue, run jobs in order, and continue after a controlled stop.
objectives: Add prepared projects with their saved module settings.
Run the queue and stop between jobs.
Find each project’s results and clear completed queue entries.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare a project and its saved module settings. For practice, use two copies of the Recruitment example in separate folders; they contain the same data and are not biological replicates.

scenes.narration: Prepare the first project in its analysis module. In Recruitment, choose Import settings and open the project’s settings CSV. The example uses two separate copies of the same measured data to practise running several jobs.
Check Source, the channel mapping and the condition labels. Save the settings you want the queue to use, then leave this project open.
Open Help, then Plate queue. The queue runs one item at a time in the listed order.
Choose Add current plate. A new row stores the current module and settings. Check its module, source and label before starting the queue.

Drag another prepared project folder onto the queue. Its saved settings identify the module, and the dropped folder becomes its source. Use separate project folders when each job needs separate output files.
Choose Run queue. The first row changes to running while later items remain queued. Watch the status and elapsed time to follow progress.
Press Stop when you want the queue to finish its current item and pause before the next one. Wait until the active job finishes.
The completed row now says success and the next row remains queued. Choose Run queue again to continue with the remaining item.

When both jobs finish, open each project’s output folder. For Recruitment, inspect the cells and wells CSV results. Use Recruitment directly when you want its figure workflow; this queue does not display or save those plots.
Choose Clear finished to remove completed entries from the list. Their project folders and saved results remain available.

lessons.title: External Masks: measure images with supplied object labels
lessons.description: Assign image and mask files, preview their pairing, then create a measured spaCR project with object tables and crops.
objectives: Assign intensity images and label masks to the correct roles.
Choose channels, output location and measurement options.
Preview the pairing, run Measure and inspect the output project.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare matching intensity images and integer-labelled masks with the same spatial dimensions. Each object needs its own positive integer label; zero is background. The example reuses two image and cell-mask pairs from the Import Project tutorial.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Import Project, then choose External Masks. Use this tool when you already have segmentation labels and want spaCR to measure the corresponding images.

Prepare matching intensity images and labelled masks. This example uses two image and cell-mask pairs. Keep each pair aligned and use filenames or metadata that let the importer match the correct field.

Click Add folder for the image folder and again for the masks. Review Use as: choose Image for intensity files and Mask for labels. Set Mask type to the compartment represented by each mask, such as Cell.
Set Use as to Ignore for any group you want to leave out. Its files stay on disk. Keep the image group and the masks required for your analysis included.
Restore Image for the example’s intensity group. Check the Image and Cell-mask assignments before choosing the destination.

Set Dst to a new project folder. Choose Layout, Z handling and Plate naming to match your files. This example uses flat layout, the first Z plane and index-based plate naming. Use acquisition metadata when original well identities must be retained.
Choose the intensity Channels to measure. This example’s TIFFs each contain one intensity plane, so select channel zero and leave Normalize off. Channel numbers refer to the files you are importing.
Choose whether to measure cytoplasm. With cell masks alone, the derived region covers the whole cell. Supply the interior compartment masks when you need them excluded from that region.

Under Object Crops, enable Save PNG and choose cell in Crop mode. Set PNG size to two hundred and twenty-four by two hundred and twenty-four. Select channel zero for this single-channel example’s PNG mapping.
Choose the measurement features you need, then enable Save measurements. Use N jobs to set concurrency. Start with a small input set while learning the settings and inspecting the resulting crops.
Enable Preview only and press Run. Check the proposed image-to-mask pairings, field count and channel layout in the plan. Correct any assignment before writing the project.
Turn off Preview only and press Run again. The tool prepares the project’s images and masks, then runs Measure to calculate object features and create the requested crops.
Inspect the intensity image beside the supplied labels. Check object boundaries, missing objects and image-to-mask alignment before interpreting the measurements.
Browse the object montage to inspect the extracted crops. Use the figure viewer to move between fields and check that the selected channels and crop size show the objects clearly.

Open measurements/measurements.db for the object tables and data for annotation crops. Keep conversion_map.csv and the source manifest with the project so imported fields remain traceable. Continue in Annotate to label the crops, or use the measurement tables in a downstream analysis.

lessons.title: Align & Stitch: plan and write an image mosaic
lessons.description: Choose image tiles, set their acquisition layout, inspect the registration plan, and write the mosaic with its coordinates.
objectives: Choose tiles and set the grid, overlap and registration channel.
Inspect the planned positions and registration quality.
Write the mosaic and retain its coordinate database.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and unzip the nine-tile example below, or prepare image tiles with known acquisition order, overlap and a useful registration channel. The example uses overlapping crops from one microscopy field to provide a practice layout.

scenes.narration: From Home’s Tools category, open Align and Stitch. Choose the tiles, review their layout with Plan, then use Write stack to create the mosaic.

Download and unzip the example below, then select its tiles folder. It contains nine overlapping crops arranged in a three-by-three grid. For your own acquisition, keep the original tile order and stage metadata available.

Set the grid to three by three, row-major order and overlap zero point two five for this example. Match these settings to your acquisition; use serpentine order when alternate rows were acquired in opposite directions.

Set Reference channel to the image plane used for registration. This example uses channel one, the second plane with zero-based numbering. Choose a channel with visible structure across overlaps; the resulting placement applies to all image channels.

Set Minimum confidence for accepting a registration and Neighbour radius for the nearby tiles to compare. The example uses zero point three and one, with feather blending across overlaps. The band-buffer budget controls memory used by the image writer.

Press Plan. Inspect the registered, nominal and unplaced tile counts and the proposed canvas size. The layout shows tile positions. Review any nominal fallback or unplaced tiles before writing the mosaic.

Click a tile to inspect its coordinates, confidence, residual and contributing pairs. Use these details to investigate unexpected positions, then adjust the registration settings and plan again if needed.
Choose an output folder and a coordinate-database path. Leave Overwrite off when creating a new result. Once the plan and destination are ready, press Write stack.

Wait for the completion summary and open the output stack. Inspect the overlaps and object boundaries in the mosaic. Keep the coordinate database and source tiles with it so downstream locations can be traced back to the acquisition.
Plattvisorn omvandlar objektmätningar till värme kartor med utrymmeskvalitetskontroll bredvid dem.
Öppna en mätdatabas eller kör mapp. Källan är bara läsbar.
Välj objekttabell, numerisk funktion och tallrik som ska visas.
Välj aggregering, färgskalar och det minsta bevis som krävs för en brunn. Talan är användbar för att upptäcka segmentering eller utsäde av skillnader.
Sätt fram visningen och jämför sedan värmekartan med rad-, kolumn-, ring- och kantdiagnostik.
Välj en brunn för att undersöka dess identifikator, objektantal, visat värde och position.
Brunnar under beviströskeln blir uttryckliga tommar snarare än vilseledande nollor.
Exporterar det nuvarande rengöringsgraden med räkningar och rumsliga annoteringar för revision eller omplanering.

lessons.title: Database Browser: filter and export measurements
lessons.description: Open a measurement database, select columns and rows, and export the result.
objectives: Open and browse a measurement table.
Select columns and filter rows.
Export the matching records.
lessons.prerequisite: Have a spaCR measurements.db file or a run folder containing one. Measure’s example project provides a database after measurement.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Database Browser to inspect and export measurement tables.
Choose measurements.db, or the run folder containing it, and open the database.
Select the table you need. Choose cell for cell measurements, or a different object table for that object’s features.
Read the total row and column counts, then inspect the displayed page. Use the page controls to move through larger tables.
Search column names to locate a feature. Select the columns you want to view and export.
Build a filter by choosing a column, an operator and a value. Apply it to select matching records across the full table.
Check the filtered row count and inspect the matching records. Adjust or clear the filter to change your selection.
Choose Export and a destination file. The export includes all matching rows and your selected columns, while keeping the source database unchanged.

lessons.title: Format Converter: preview and convert image files
lessons.description: Select a source folder, check the target names and channel assignments, then convert images and resume completed work.
objectives: Choose source and destination folders with the correct acquisition layout.
Preview target names, fields and channel assignments.
Convert the files and use Resume for completed fields.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare a folder of supported image files and retain their acquisition metadata. You can practise with the two TIFF images used in the Import Project tutorial. Set the layout and Z handling for your own acquisition.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Import Project and choose Format Converter. Use it to prepare image files and filenames for the next analysis step.
Use the converter’s Source, Destination, Preview and Convert controls. Preview displays the planned source-to-target mapping so you can inspect the assignments before writing files.
Choose the folder containing your source images. This example uses two single-channel TIFFs. Keep the original acquisition metadata available when checking the converted names.
Choose a new destination folder. The converter writes the new images there together with a mapping file; retain your original images separately.

Set Layout to match your folders. Choose images directly in source for the example’s flat folder, and select the plate-naming rule you need. For a plate-and-well directory tree, choose its corresponding layout.

Choose how to handle Z planes. Keep every plane when you need the full stack, use maximum projection for a projected image, or choose the first plane when that is the intended input. This example contains one plane per file.

Press Preview. Inspect every source-to-target assignment, including plate, well, field and channel. Indexed names are assigned identities; use the original metadata to confirm which experimental conditions they represent.

Review From field and From channel alongside the target names. Channel indexes in arrays and channel numbers in filenames can use different conventions. Check that each target contains the image plane you intend to analyse.
If a mapping is wrong, change the source layout or conversion settings and preview again. The preview table is read-only.
Press Convert and read the completion summary for converted, failed and skipped files. Open a converted image to inspect its dimensions and channels before continuing to segmentation or measurement.
Keep conversion_map.csv with the converted images. It records source and target paths, assigned identities and conversion status. Retain the original acquisition metadata alongside it.

For a later run with the same source, plan and destination, enable Resume. Compatible completed fields can be reused. Read the summary to see which files were converted and which were already present.

lessons.title: Import Project: bring images, masks and measurements into spaCR
lessons.description: Choose matching images, instance masks and measurement tables, review their mapping, and create a spaCR project.
objectives: Match images, masks and measurement rows.
Review and save the column mapping.
Import the project and inspect its outputs.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare corresponding image files, instance-label masks and a measurement CSV. Keep each field’s original plate and well identity, and use documented measurement units.

scenes.narration: From Home’s Data category, open Import. Use this screen to bring existing images, instance masks and measurements into a spaCR project.

The header also opens Import Images, Format Converter and External Masks. Choose the tool that matches your starting files; this walkthrough uses images, masks and an existing measurement table together.
Choose the image folder. The example uses two microscopy fields with one intensity channel and matching cell labels. Keep a record of each file’s original plate, well and field.
Choose the Cell mask folder and press Add. Each object needs its own integer label. Add further mask classes when you have corresponding labels for the same fields.
Choose the measurement CSV. Match ImageNumber to each field and ObjectNumber to its mask label. Use both identifiers to distinguish objects across fields.
Enter micrometres per pixel when you know the calibration; otherwise leave it blank. Check that area and intensity columns retain their documented units.
Press Preview to inspect the proposed column mapping and joins before creating the project. Review the suggested foreign-prefixed names and their scientific meaning.
Select a target cell and press F two to edit its name. A reserved-name conflict disables Import when Refuse the import is selected; choose a distinct target name or use the Rename policy.
Read the join report and resolve unmatched rows or objects. In the example, all one hundred and three measurement rows match mask objects.
Give the imported area a clear name, such as foreign reviewed area pixels squared. Review the source, target, transform and units together.
Use Save mapping to keep the reviewed column definitions as a CSV. Keep the mapping with your images, masks, measurement table and acquisition identities.
Use Load mapping to reuse saved definitions. Review the resulting plan whenever source columns, labels or units differ.
Press Import and read the completion report. The example writes two image files, two masks and two merged arrays, with one hundred and three rows in each of two object tables.
Open the project and inspect the imported measurements. The foreign columns table records their origin. Use Measure when you want spaCR to calculate new features from the images.

Keep the conversion map with the project and check its plate, well and field assignments. Generic file names may receive new coordinates, so resolve their original identities before plate-level analysis.
Continue in Database Browser to inspect the tables or in Annotate to review object crops. Retain the reviewed mapping with the completed project.

lessons.title: Batch Runner: configure and run a queue
lessons.description: Add module settings, arrange dependencies, run jobs, and inspect their separate logs.
objectives: Add jobs with their settings and dependencies.
Save, run and continue the queue.
Inspect each job’s log and outputs.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare the input data and exported settings JSON for each job. The example runs three image conversions into separate output folders.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Batch runner. Use it to queue module jobs with their settings files, execution order and separate logs.
Choose the module and click Choose settings. For this example, select convert and the JSON settings for the first microscopy field.
Check the source and destination in the settings, add a descriptive label, then click Add job. Use a separate output folder for each conversion.

For the second job, enter convert one in After to make it depend on the first. Add a setting override when this job needs a different value. Set any input paths explicitly; a dependency controls order.
Add further jobs and review their identifiers, labels and dependencies. Select a row to load its configuration into the editor.
Use the move controls to arrange jobs. A dependency must appear before the job that needs it; read any validation message and correct the order.
Click Validate after arranging the queue. Resolve the listed problems until Run queue becomes available.
Choose On failure to continue with independent jobs or stop at the first failure. Set Stop after to limit consecutive failures.
Click Save queue to store the plan as JSON. Use Load queue to reopen it later, keeping the referenced settings files and inputs available.
Click Run queue. To pause between jobs, press Stop; the current job finishes and the remaining jobs stay unrun.
Click Run queue again to continue with the remaining jobs. Watch each row’s status as the queue progresses.
Select a row to read its log and inspect errors or output paths. For the conversion example, check the reported field and channel identifiers.
Open each output folder and inspect the converted images and conversion record. Keep the queue JSON, settings and logs with the results.

lessons.title: Distributed Jobs: configure an execution target
lessons.description: Create an execution profile and prepare a module job for another workstation or cluster.
objectives: Create a profile for your execution target.
Configure paths and backend options.
Prepare submission and inspect job status.
lessons.prerequisite: Arrange access to a target with spaCR, its dependencies and your input data. Export the module settings you intend to run. Replace the illustrative host and paths shown here with your own.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Distributed jobs. Start by creating an execution profile for the workstation or cluster you want to use.
Install compatible spaCR dependencies on the target and make the input data available there. Set up SSH keys or your provider’s command-line authentication outside spaCR.
Choose New profile. Enter a descriptive name and select the backend. Complete the required fields shown by the form.
For SSH, enter your host, remote work directory and spaCR runner. Save the profile, then reopen it whenever you need to update these settings.
Set the local and remote dataset roots when the same data has different absolute paths on the two machines. This rewrites settings paths; arrange shared storage or copy the files separately.
For Slurm, choose the partition, time limit and accelerator request supported by your cluster. Keep the host and directory settings appropriate for its login environment.
For a cloud or custom command, enter submit, status and cancel argument templates, plus log retrieval if needed. Include the required settings and external-ID placeholders shown by the controls.
Save the changes you want to retain, or use Cancel to leave the profile unchanged. Poll interval sets how frequently to check job status.

Select the profile, module and its exported settings, then use Submit when the target is ready. Monitor status and logs in the job table. Use Cancel job to stop a selected job, and inspect its results at the configured output location.

lessons.title: Classifier Evaluation: inspect predictions and errors
lessons.description: Load a saved evaluation bundle, inspect leakage and confusion counts, and filter predictions for review.
objectives: Load a bundle and review leakage.
Inspect confusion counts and confidence groups.
Filter predictions and locate saved figures.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and unzip the linked saved-results example. It contains predictions, tables and figures; crops require your matching experiment in Annotate. The example shares wells between training and test data, so use it to learn the inspector rather than estimate independent-well accuracy.

scenes.narration: Open Classify, then Classifier Evaluation. Use this inspector to explore a saved evaluation bundle after producing predictions.
Download and unzip the example below. Click Browse and choose the folder containing evaluation manifest dot json.
Read Summary for the number of predictions and the recorded class names. The example contains two hundred thirty-four predictions across two classes.

Open Leakage audit before interpreting accuracy. This example flags wells shared between training and test data. For an independent-well evaluation, prepare a split with separate wells and rerun training and evaluation.
Open Confusion matrix. Rows are recorded classes and columns are predictions. The diagonal shows agreement; off-diagonal cells identify disagreements to review.
Click a disagreement cell to list its examples. The selected cell contains eleven disagreements, grouped by confidence.

Change Confidence threshold to choose which disagreements enter the high-confidence list. Raising it from zero point seven five to zero point nine five leaves two in the high list and nine in the low list.
Review the selected examples alongside their images and annotations. Use the displayed explanations as prompts for investigation, and check the evidence before changing labels.
Open Per-plate metrics to compare results by plate. This example has one plate; a multi-plate bundle provides separate rows for comparison.
Open Calibration to compare predicted probability with observed class frequency. Check each bin’s count when interpreting the differences.
Open Predictions and type a sample or well identifier to filter the records. In the example, r five underscore c two selects one well’s predictions.
Clear the filter to restore all records. To open crops in your own project, first load the matching experiment in Annotate; the downloadable results example contains no crops.
Find the saved calibration and confusion figures in the bundle folder. Check labels and readability before using them in a report.
Keep the leakage audit with reported metrics. Use Training Runs to compare saved training progress, and return to Annotate when image or label review is needed.

lessons.title: Run History: inspect past jobs and restore settings
lessons.description: Find saved runs, inspect settings and logs, and load a previous configuration into its module.
objectives: Find runs using filters and search.
Inspect saved settings, files and problems.
Restore settings for a new run.
lessons.prerequisite: Complete a spaCR job to create a local run record. The example browses records from conversion, Recruitment and Regression runs.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Run history to browse the run records saved on this computer.
Click Refresh to load available records. Select a run to inspect its details, and drag the divider if you need more room.
Choose a module and status, then enter a search term to narrow the list. For example, select convert and Success to find completed conversions.
Open Files and models for recorded input and output details. Runs that skipped file hashing can have an empty inventory; use the output paths in settings or logs to find their results.
Clear or adjust the filters if the table is empty. Search terms and status selections work together.
Select a Recruitment run and read Overview for its elapsed time and recorded file counts. These summarize that saved execution.
Open Settings to inspect its source folder, channels and object filters. Scroll through the saved configuration before deciding to reuse it.
Open Files and models to inspect recorded paths, sizes and hashes. Keep the referenced project files available when you need to revisit the analysis.
Open Environment for recorded software versions and seeds. Use Copy path to locate the run’s journal folder.
Open Warnings and failure to read warnings attached to a completed run. Investigate relevant warnings before using its results.
Choose Failed to find unsuccessful jobs. Read the traceback and software versions when diagnosing a problem or preparing a bug report.
Return to the desired run and choose Load settings in module. Review the restored controls and current input paths before pressing Run.
Keep the journals you need with your project records. Use Clear all only when you intend to delete run records. Open Report to create a project summary.

lessons.title: Classify: choose a model and explore its results
lessons.description: Choose image or feature classification, load example data, inspect prediction results and open the related tools inside Classify.
objectives: Choose Computer Vision for images or Tabular Machine Learning for measurements.
Start with test data and follow the matching training walkthrough.
Inspect predictions and open evaluation, feature and training tools.
lessons.prerequisite: Open Classify from Home. Use Load test data for an example project. For your own project, prepare object crops or measured features and class labels from annotations or experimental metadata.

scenes.narration: Open Classify from Home. Start by choosing the classifier family. The image and tabular lessons linked here each walk through a complete example.
Choose Computer Vision to learn from object images. Choose Tabular Machine Learning to learn from measured feature columns. Measure provides these inputs, and Annotate lets you add object labels.
For the tabular example, click Load test data and choose Load. Select your class labels and feature settings, then follow the tabular lesson to train the model and save predictions.

After the tabular run, inspect the prediction heatmap and saved object scores. Objects with missing required measurements may remain unscored. Check the evaluation results to decide whether to revise your labels, features or model settings.

For image classification, follow the Computer Vision lesson to prepare labelled crops, choose a model, and set the training, validation and test splits. After training, inspect the evaluation figures and saved predictions.
Open Classifier Evaluation from the top-right tools. Select a saved evaluation bundle to inspect predictions, metrics and the data split.

Open Explain CV to relate an image classifier’s predictions to measured features. Supply the image prediction results and the corresponding measurements, then inspect which features explain the scores.
Open Activation to view which image regions influence model responses. Select the trained checkpoint and use the same image channels and preprocessing as during training.
Open Training Runs to compare saved training histories. Select runs with compatible metrics and data splits, then inspect their learning curves and settings.
Open Feature Explorer to compare measured features between selected groups. Choose the groups and filters, then inspect the feature ranking and plots.

Keep your trained model, predictions and evaluation results in the run folder. You can use object scores in Regression together with matching guide counts. The linked module lessons show the next steps.

lessons.title: Curate: edit masks and tracks
lessons.description: Practise brush edits, track splitting and joining, and save the corrected files.
objectives: Edit a label mask with the brush and undo controls.
Split, join and save tracks.
Preserve source files and curation history.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the synthetic practice archive and work on copies. Keep separate backups of masks and their .curation.json sidecars before reopening: saving a reopened mask currently replaces its earlier edit log.

scenes.narration: Open Make Masks, then Curate to edit label masks and tracks. Download the synthetic practice example below and keep an untouched copy.
Browse to the example’s integer-label TIFF. Each object has its own label, with zero reserved for background. Use the TIFF example for this walkthrough.
Set Brush radius to eight and click New to select a new label. Click an empty part of the practice image to paint a small region.
Click Undo stroke to remove the last brush edit. Paint again and inspect the result before saving.
Click Save mask to write the working TIFF and its curation sidecar. Before reopening, preserve both files in a new backup folder; the download includes a checkpoint script for this step.
Keep each session’s backup and edit notes. Reopening a mask starts a new in-memory log, and another save replaces its sidecar with that session’s history.
Browse to the tracks CSV and select tracks to review. Join accepts tracks with non-overlapping frame ranges; an overlap produces a message to resolve first.
Select track two, set Split at frame to four, and click Split. The later frames move to a new track while the earlier frames retain the original identifier.
Select the two non-overlapping halves and click Join to combine them. Click Save tracks to write the CSV and its separate curation sidecar.
Use Delete only for tracks you intend to remove. To discard an unsaved change, reopen the last saved CSV.
Inspect the reopened tracks and saved history. Keep originals and reasons for edits, and rerun any downstream analysis affected by corrected masks or trajectories.

lessons.title: Illumination: estimate and inspect a correction model
lessons.description: Choose image channels, estimate an illumination field, inspect its QC figure, and reuse the saved model.
objectives: Select representative fields and intensity channels.
Estimate and inspect an illumination model.
Reuse the model in Mask or Measure.
lessons.prerequisite: Use a merged image folder with representative fields from each acquisition group. The example uses the sixteen fields from Measure’s downloaded plate example. Know which stored planes contain intensities and which contain labels.

scenes.narration: Open Measure, then Illumination to estimate a correction model for uneven image brightness.
Set Source to the merged folder containing image arrays. Use representative fields from your acquisition; the example uses sixteen fields from one plate.
Set Channels to the stored intensity planes you want to correct. The example uses channel zero. Check your channel mapping and exclude label-mask planes.
Enable Illumination correction before estimating a field. When it is off, Run completes without creating a correction model.

Choose an estimator and its settings. For the polynomial example, use degree four and leave Illumination model empty to estimate a new field. Inspect the result for structures that belong to cells rather than illumination.
Enable Illumination per plate to fit separate acquisition groups. Set Maximum fields to a representative sample; the example includes all sixteen available fields.
Set Illumination dark from your camera calibration when available. It is an additive offset in raw counts; zero is the example setting.
Enable Illumination QC and choose a missing-model policy. With error selected, a missing plate correction stops processing so you can resolve it.
Press Run and read the saved model path in the console. This step estimates the model; enable it in a subsequent analysis to apply the correction.
Open the saved illumination QC PNG in the illumination folder. Use an image viewer if it does not appear in the Figures panel.
Inspect the estimated illumination field for smooth brightness variation and unwanted cell-shaped structure. Correction subtracts the dark offset and divides by this mean-one field.
Compare the before and after radial profiles. Use additional fields to assess how well the correction works beyond the images used to fit it.

To reuse the model, set its path and enable correction in the intended Mask or Measure workflow. Keep its channels, plate identities and settings with it, and avoid correcting the same intensities twice.

lessons.title: Data Manager: inspect usage, clean up and archive
lessons.description: Review project storage, preview a cleanup plan, and move a project to an archive destination.
objectives: Inspect project disk usage.
Review and apply a cleanup plan.
Move and rescan an archived project.
lessons.prerequisite: Use a completed spaCR project and keep an independent backup before cleanup. The example uses a copy of the project produced by External Masks.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Data manager. Choose a completed project to inspect its storage and plan cleanup or archiving.
Click Choose project and select the project root. Read Usage for its files, disk space and registered artifacts.
Open Prune and select the artifact types to consider. Leave measurement databases and model weights unchecked when you want to keep them, then click Show what can be deleted.
Review the proposed files, space saving and recovery information. The example selects the object-crop folder. Keep the inputs and settings needed to regenerate anything you remove.
Click Delete to review the final file list. Deletion cannot be undone, so check the paths and your backup before acknowledging the plan.
Use Cancel if you want to keep the files or revise the selection. Acknowledging the list enables the final Delete action.
Confirm Delete when the plan is correct. Read the result for the number of removed files and space recovered.
Review the updated Usage scan. Removed artifacts may remain listed as missing with their recorded recipe; regenerate them through the appropriate module when needed.
Open Archive and choose an empty destination outside the source project. Click Show what would move and inspect both paths.
Click Move to review the confirmation. Archive moves the project, so keep any separate backup you need before proceeding.
Confirm Yes to move the project. Keep the manifest at the destination and the archive log left at the original location.
Select the destination as the project and scan it again. Check the moved files and update any external references that still point to the old location.
Use Database Browser to inspect measurement tables, Report to make a project summary, and Data Manager for storage maintenance. Keep the archive records with your project documentation.

lessons.title: Project Browser: find and inspect projects
lessons.description: Search project folders, inspect recorded stages, and identify the next tool to open.
objectives: Discover projects using roots and search depth.
Inspect artifacts and recorded stages.
Choose the next relevant tool.
lessons.prerequisite: Choose folders containing your spaCR projects. Completed External Masks and Format Converter examples can be used for practice.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Project browser to find project folders and inspect their recorded outputs.
Click Add folder and choose a search root. Depth zero checks that folder itself; increase the depth when projects are inside subfolders.
Set Depth to one and click Scan to include folders immediately below the root. Inspect the resulting project rows.
Read State and Stage alongside the files found on disk. A folder without an artifact registry may show unknown even when it contains converted images.
Add further search roots to include other projects. Select a row to inspect it; if details are blank after a rescan, select another row and return.
Drag the divider to widen the details. Review recorded artifacts, unregistered files and the source of the last-run timestamp.
Open Stages to see which expected outputs are present. Use What could run next to choose a relevant workflow, then check that module’s required inputs.
Click a column heading such as Size to sort projects. Click it again to reverse the order.
Adjust Depth and scan again when you need a narrower or wider search. A directly selected project remains discoverable at depth zero.
Select a root and click Remove to stop searching it. This removes the search location from the list while leaving its files on disk.
Open Run History for job records, Database Browser for measurements, or Data Manager for cleanup and archiving. Use the relevant module tutorial to continue the analysis.

lessons.title: Napari Bridge: edit and return a label mask
lessons.description: Open an image and mask in napari, edit labels, and save the corrected mask back to spaCR.
objectives: Open corresponding image and label files.
Edit and undo changes in napari.
Return and inspect the saved mask.
lessons.prerequisite: Install the optional napari dependency and unzip the synthetic example into a new folder. Keep an untouched backup: Take the mask back overwrites the selected working mask. Close and reopen the viewer between saved editing rounds.

scenes.narration: Open Make Masks, then Napari Bridge. Use it to edit an existing label mask with its intensity image as a reference. Keep an untouched backup of the mask.
Download and unzip the synthetic example. Choose mask dot tif for Mask and image dot tif for Image, then press Open in napari.
Select the mask Labels layer in napari. Label zero is background; each object label has a display colour. Make edits on the labels layer.
Return to spaCR and use Take the mask back to import the viewer’s current labels. If you have made no changes, the status reports that the mask is unchanged.
For practice, select label eighteen, choose Fill, and click the object labelled two. Inspect the changed label before importing it.
Use Undo to reverse the last viewer edit. Repeat the Fill operation when you are ready to keep the change.
Click Take the mask back in spaCR. Review the changed-pixel count, then inspect the saved mask and its correction-history sidecar.
Click Close viewer and reopen the mask before the next editing round. This makes the saved mask the starting point for subsequent corrections.
After the next edit, take the mask back and inspect the result again. Close the viewer when finished, keep the correction history, and rerun measurements affected by the changed labels.

lessons.title: Barcode QC: inspect read depth and choose a cutoff
lessons.description: Load mapped counts, review well and guide coverage, and compare abundance thresholds.
objectives: Choose count inputs and QC settings.
Inspect coverage and positional effects.
Compare thresholds and keep the resulting tables and plots.
lessons.prerequisite: Use plate_1_unique_combinations.csv from the downloaded example-screen data in the Regression tutorial, or your own mapped count table. Choose a new output folder. Supply mapping-QC and barcode-reference files when you need checks that depend on unmapped reads or the expected library.

scenes.narration: Open Map Barcodes, then Barcode QC. Start from a mapped count table; the linked Regression example provides one for practice.
Set Count data to your count table and choose a new output destination. The example contains mapped reads across three hundred eighty-four wells.
Set Target gRNAs per well from your experimental design and choose the summary method used to derive the cutoff. The example uses five and median.
Set Starved read fraction to flag wells with low reads relative to the plate median. The example uses zero point one. Review flagged wells before excluding them.
Enable Plot and Save, then press Run. Add mapping-QC or reference inputs when you want their corresponding checks; the count table alone describes observed mapped reads.
Read the completion log and saved output paths. Investigate errors against the selected inputs before using the results.
Open barcode QC dot PNG and threshold sweep dot PNG from the output folder. Use an image viewer if the Figures panel is empty.
Inspect read depth, row and column effects, and guide representation. Compare with a reference library when you need to identify expected guides that are missing entirely.
Inspect the threshold sweep. In this example, a cutoff near one point two one percent of each well’s reads gives a median of five guides while retaining about fifty-eight percent of mapped reads.

Compare retained reads, retained wells and wells above the guide target as the cutoff changes. Choose a cutoff appropriate to your design; the guide target does not establish single-guide attribution.
Keep the recommendation, sweep table, plots and settings with the source counts. Use the chosen cutoff consistently in the downstream analysis and record the reason for your choice.

lessons.title: Hit List: granska kandidater i ett tydligt externt hjälpfönster
lessons.description: Utforska verkliga Hit List-filter och exporter med oförändrade Regression-resultat och en uttryckligt beskriven omväg runt den dolda panelen.
objectives: Skilja den trasiga inbyggda genvägen från det externa hjälpprogrammet.
Tolka rangordnade kandidater utan att hävda signifikanta upptäckter.
Filtrera, återställa och exportera de faktiska raderna.
lessons.prerequisite: Packa upp Hit_List_real_results_companion.zip, aktivera spaCR-miljön, kör python hit_list_companion.py och välj results med Browse. Programmet använder oförändrad HitListScreen; det reparerar inte navigeringen eller ansluter Investigate. Arkivet innehåller ursprungliga resultat, inte ett helt projekt: 325 gener, 434 guiderader och inga gener med q <= .05. Standardiserade marginaleffekter är inte samtidigt skattade multivariabla koefficienter. Saknade intervall är otillgängliga. n_obs=0 anger inte verkligt brunnsstöd: wells_with_gene i results_gene.csv ligger mellan 2 och 48. Metadata-kopplingar, penaliserad rangordning och Investigate ingår inte. Ingen träning, ny regression, GPU eller förfrågan till en AI-leverantör behövs. API: spacr.hits.build_hit_list och HitList.filter/write_csv/to_markdown/to_html.

scenes.narration: Hit List hör till Regression. I den här versionen väljer ett klick på Hits en sida i en dold panel, så listan visas inte. Handledningen visar begränsningen öppet. Nästa fönster är ett externt hjälpprogram, inte bevis för att den inbyggda genvägen har reparerats.

Packa upp det länkade exemplet, aktivera spaCR-miljön och kör det medföljande Hit List-hjälpskriptet. Det märkta fönstret öppnar spaCRs befintliga widget utan ändrade beräkningar. Klicka på Browse och välj results. Regressionen körs inte om, och Investigate-integrationen är inte ansluten här.

Originalexemplet laddar 325 gener. Dubbelklicka på kolumngränserna om värden klipps. Läs effektriktning, rått P, korrigerat q och guideöverensstämmelse separat. Saknade konfidensintervall är otillgängliga. Effekterna är standardiserade marginaleffekter; noll i det exporterade observationsantalet är inte det verkliga antalet stödjande brunnar.

Sätt Max q till 0,05. Inga gener återstår eftersom det minsta gen-q-värdet är cirka 0,271. En tom filtrerad tabell betyder inte importfel. Återställ Max q till ett för att få tillbaka kandidaterna, utan att kalla dem upptäckter.

Minimum guides på två behåller 117 gener med minst två testade guiderader. Det räknar tillgänglig evidens, inte alla guider som ursprungligen utformades. Filtret ändrar den visade delmängden utan att räkna om korrektionen för multipla tester.

Minimum agreement på ett behåller därefter 57 gener vars testade guider alla delar geneffektens tecken. Överensstämmelse bevisar varken signifikans eller orsakssamband. Sammanfattningen visar fortfarande noll signifikanta gener med samstämmigt stöd, trots att dessa kandidatrader har överensstämmande guider.

Hide controls tar bort en kontrollrad och lämnar 56 kandidater. Återställ den före exporten. Dolda kontroller innebär inte att modellen anpassas om eller att korrektionsfamiljen ändras; behåll deras identiteter när analysen tolkas.

Med övriga filter nollställda visar Direction up positiva effekter. En minsta absolut effekt på 0,1 lämnar 16 rader. Detta är illustrativa visningsval, inte rekommenderade trösklar. Återställ riktning och effekt före sökning eller jämförelse med en annan delmängd.

Sök efter en registrerad identifierare för att granska en faktisk rad. En sökning utan träffar tömmer tabellen; den kända identifieraren återställer raden och en tom sökning hela populationen. Filtreringen är reversibel. Annotationsimport och Investigate behöver egna kontroller.

För export återställs två guider, full överensstämmelse, kontroller inkluderade och tom sökning. Alla tre exporter innehåller samma 57 kandidater här. Markdown och HTML avrundar tal; CSV bevarar numeriska detaljer. Spara filtren separat eftersom filerna inte registrerar alla inställningar.

Nollställ filtren för att återfå alla 325 gener. Håll exporterade delmängder åtskilda från oförändrade original och kalla inte icke-signifikanta kandidater validerade träffar. Python erbjuder samma läsare och filter; kontrollera formatspecifika radgränser för större listor.

lessons.title: Methods & Results: draft and export a run report
lessons.description: Select a completed run, build its report, review the recorded settings and results, and export Markdown.
objectives: Select the project, run journal and matching result folder.
Build a digest and review the Methods, Results and Caveats tabs.
Copy the report text or export Markdown with the run digest.
lessons.prerequisite: Complete the Regression example first. Keep its project folder, run journal and guide_permutation results together. Review inferred settings, analysis versions and statistical thresholds before using the generated text in a report.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Regression, then Methods and Results. Use this tool to draft a report from a completed analysis. This walkthrough continues with the saved run from the Regression example.

Choose the project folder, the run journal and the matching regression-results folder. Leave Classifier empty for this regression example. Confirm that all selected files belong to the run you want to describe.
Click Build digest, then read the Methods and Results tabs. Check the analysis version against the saved run environment; the exporter version can differ from the version that performed the analysis.

Read Caveats and compare seed entries by name with the saved settings. A permutation seed and a global seed refer to different generators. Leave an unrecorded historical seed unknown when editing the report.
Open Run digest to inspect the structured settings and source records. Compare them with the prose and review warnings about missing reports or inferred defaults before sharing the draft.

In Results, inspect effect sizes and corrected q-values together. This example has no genes below a q-value threshold of zero point zero five. Describe the listed rows as ranked candidates when editing a heading that calls them hits.
Click Copy sections to copy the displayed Methods and Results. Review the copied text against the source records. Use Export Markdown when you also need the structured run digest.
Click Export Markdown and choose a new filename. The file contains both report sections and the run digest as an appendix. Keep an original draft and save your reviewed revisions separately.

Draft with AI is optional and sends the digest to your configured provider. Review its contents before using that option, then check any generated text against the saved analysis. You can also use build_digest, render_methods and render_results from Python.

lessons.title: Run Compare: compare saved runs
lessons.description: Choose two saved runs, inspect settings and count differences, and check available result comparisons.
objectives: Select baseline and comparison runs.
Inspect settings and count differences.
Locate available result comparisons.
lessons.prerequisite: Download and unzip the linked snapshots. Follow its README to run prepare_run_compare_download.py in your spaCR environment with a new destination folder. For your own comparisons, preserve each run’s outputs before they are overwritten.

scenes.narration: From Home’s Data category, open Run Compare to inspect outputs recorded for two runs.
Download and unzip the snapshot example. Follow its README to run the preparation script with a new destination folder.
Click Browse and select the prepared comparison folder. Keep original projects and their run snapshots available for your own comparisons.
Choose a baseline run as A and the comparison run as B, then click Compare. Check their module names and recorded versions.
Enable Show unchanged settings to include matching values. Expand entries to inspect the configuration used by each run.
Open Counts to compare object totals. Delta is B minus A. The example has matching counts; inspect the relevant images and measurements when you need to understand a difference.
Open Hits when both runs have registered regression results. The example contains Measure snapshots, so no hit comparison is available.
Choose two distinct runs. If the same run is selected on both sides, use the warning to correct the selection.
Keep both output snapshots and the settings that explain their differences. Use Run History for individual logs and Regression for the underlying hit results.

lessons.title: Control Charts: monitor controls across plates
lessons.description: Load a campaign table, select controls and baseline limits, inspect alerts, and export the plotted points.
objectives: Choose the measurement and control population.
Set the baseline and alert rules.
Inspect alerts and export chart points.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the synthetic campaign CSV below, or prepare a well-level table with plate identity, run order, a measurement and control labels. The example illustrates thirty plates with programmed drift.

scenes.narration: Open QC, then Control Charts to monitor repeated controls across a campaign. The practice CSV uses synthetic plates and a programmed drift.
Download the example CSV below, click Load table and select it. It contains thirty plates, each with three wells for each control type and three sample wells.
Match Plate, Run order, Measurement and Control column to the table. Under Control is, select neg for the negative controls. An empty selection includes all rows.
Choose Sigma from to control the variation estimator. Auto uses the subgroup estimator here, because each plate contains three selected control wells.
Choose Rules for the alerts you want to inspect. The example uses Limits only to focus on points outside the three-sigma limits. Changing a setting redraws the chart.
Set Baseline plates to twenty. The first twenty plates establish limits for the series. Read the report and rule table to locate flagged later plates.
To inspect positive controls, clear neg and select pos. Review their means and limits separately, then return to neg to continue the example.
Adjust Baseline plates when your planned reference period differs. The tool requires at least eight plates; choose a stable baseline appropriate to the assay.
Click Export points and choose a CSV destination. It saves plate identities, means, subgroup sizes, limits, baseline membership and fired rules.
Keep the input CSV, selected controls and baseline settings with the exported points. Use the flagged plate identities to investigate acquisition or assay changes.

lessons.title: Pipeline Graph: inspect outputs and dependencies
lessons.description: Open a project’s artifact graph, inspect missing outputs, and copy its dependency diagram.
objectives: Open the artifact graph for a project.
Inspect paths, states and dependencies.
Copy the diagram and refresh its records.
lessons.prerequisite: Choose a spaCR project with registered outputs. The External Masks example supplies measurements and crops; the Data Manager lesson shows how a removed artifact appears.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Pipeline graph to inspect a project’s recorded outputs and dependencies.
Browse to the project folder. If the graph is empty, check whether that folder has registered artifacts; existing files can be present without registry records.
Choose the measured project to display its artifact boxes. The example includes measurements, crops and a resource log, with a removed crop folder marked missing.
Click an artifact and widen the details with the divider. Inspect its path, role, run identifier, production time and software version.
Select a Missing artifact to find its recorded path. Its displayed size describes the saved record, so check the actual location when investigating absent files.
